title: batch-edgecase-nsight-walkthrough-2025-12
content:
High-level summary:

Short version: during microbatch boundary transitions in production-like workloads we observed recurring tail-latency spikes (~200-800us) that correlate with small but consistent gaps in the GPU kernel timeline. This doc walks through the Nsight captures, quick repro steps, intermediate microbenchmarks, and concrete experiments to validate hypotheses (stream sync, graph replay fragmentation, and allocator contention).

Why I care: these spikes show up in 99.9th percentile for the chat streaming endpoint and are responsible for a non-trivial proportion of SLO breaches during synthetic P95->P99 ramp tests. Fixing them improves tail latency without increasing cost (no extra GPUs).

Test rig and config used for captures:
- Model: vicuna-like small serve variant (16k chunked KV, 8-bit quantized path)
- Hardware: A100-SXM4 40GB (single GPU host for these runs)
- CUDA: 12.1, driver 535.x; Nsight Systems 2025.3, Nsight Compute 2025.2 for kernel breakdowns
- Runtime build: serve-runtime main @ 2025-11-29 (PR 678 has minor batching refactor; capture before/after runs available)
- Batcher config: dynamic microbatching with horizon=16, max_microbatch=8, preferred_batch_size=512 tokens; async-copy enabled; cuda-graph warmup enabled after N cold requests
- NVTX: we annotate: SERVICE_ENTRY, BATCHER_HANDOFF, KERNEL_LAUNCH_PREP, CUDA_GRAPH_REPLAY, POST_REPLAY_SYNC

Repro steps (short):
1) Start a single GPU node with the build and the config above.
2) Run the synthetic ramp runner: 200 concurrent clients, tokens/sec ramp to ~45k tokens/s across clients. Use deterministic seed to ensure repeatable input-length distribution.
3) Capture Nsight for a 60s steady window once cuda-graph warmups complete (~after ~30s).
4) Run microbench variants: change horizon 8/16/32; toggle async-copy; toggle prewarm graphs.

Key observations from primary Nsight timeline (video + API trace):
- Recurrent narrow gaps on the GPU timeline that align to the end of KERNEL_LAUNCH_PREP NVTX region then immediately before CUDA_GRAPH_REPLAY. Measured gap duration: 220-760us, median ~350us across captures.
- During gaps the SM occupancy drops from 68-72% down to 6-12% (measured via sample points in Nsight).
- Kernel durations for the attention kernels themselves are stable and unchanged; the extraneous overhead is outside the kernel (host-side prep / replay injection).
- NVTX stack shows that at gap boundaries we do a short cudaStreamSynchronize on the low-priority stream while high-priority copy stream is still draining.
- CUDA graph replay sometimes emits two smaller kernel launches instead of one fused launch when the microbatch crosses a grid-size threshold (i.e., when token count pushes block dims into the next allocation bucket). This appears as fragmentation in the timeline (one kernel, tiny gap, another kernel).
- Persistent kernel experiment: enabling persistent-kernel mode reduces both gap frequency and gap duration by ~65% in our test.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Race between async-copy stream and low-priority launch stream causes host synchronization (cudaStreamSynchronize) to spin-wait & create visible GPU idle intervals. The runtime currently uses a conservative sync to ensure KV cache coherence.
2) CUDA graph replay fragmentation: grid-size bucketing + fallback path in the launcher introduces an extra host dispatch for the second fragment. Overhead small but visible at microbatch scale.
3) Allocator/driver stalls on memory mapping or context switching when graphs are re-compiled or when graph capture is partially invalidated (rare).

Evidence supporting hypotheses:
- Stream race: Nsight shows consistent alignment of gap to the POST_REPLAY_SYNC NVTX marker. Removing the sync (in controlled local build) eliminates the gap but causes occasional correctness failures for the KV cache (we can reproduce an off-by-one in cache pointer).
- Fragmentation: kernel size histogram from Nsight indicates ~12% of microbatches produce two kernels vs one; those two-kernel cases almost always have an inner tiny gap between launches.
- Allocator: rare full-driver stalls correlate with graph-capture windows triggered by dynamic shapes; turning off on-demand graph recapture reduces frequency to near-zero.

Quick microbench (what I ran to isolate):
- Synthetic single-op replay: run repeated single microbatch with fixed token length across 10k iterations, capturing latency distribution. Toggles tested: stream-priority (high/normal), prewarm graphs (on/off), persistent-kernel (on/off). Results: persistent-kernel + prewarm graphs reduces 99.9th by 2.1x vs baseline; stream-priority tweaks reduce variance but not median.

Detailed numbers (representative):
- Baseline (horizon=16): median per-microbatch = 1.85ms, p99 = 3.4ms, p99.9 = 6.1ms
- With persistent kernels enabled: median = 1.78ms, p99 = 2.9ms, p99.9 = 2.5ms (note: for p99.9 the value decreased dramatically because many tails were eliminated)
- With stream-priority bump (copy stream -> high): p99.9 improved modestly (6.1ms -> 4.9ms), but some copy stalls pushed host CPU overhead up by ~10%
- With graph prewarm and disabled on-demand recapture: tail improvements similar to persistent kernels but slightly less consistent when input length distribution varied.

Risk/observed regressions when applying mitigations locally:
- Removing the conservative sync without fixing the underlying KV coherence leads to occasional incorrect KV hits; we cannot remove it blindly.
- Persistent kernel mode increases GPU resident memory footprint (~200-400MB), so on small-card hosts this could increase OOM risk.
- Forcing stream priority to high for the copy stream increased contention with other latency-sensitive kernels when co-located on multi-tenant hosts. This suggests a config knob at node-level rather than global change.

Actionable experiments (next 2 weeks):
1) Implement a targeted pre-warm + pinned replay path: when microbatch sizes are within known buckets, use a compiled graph variant that is kept alive and swapped without recapture. Measure tail impact. (owner: Evan)
2) Replace the broad cudaStreamSynchronize with a finer-grained fence that checks KV cache timestamps + lightweight spin. Aim: remove full host sync for the common fast-path. Add correctness asserts to detect KV pointer drift. (owner: Priya)
3) Add a telemetry metric: "graph_fragment_rate" (percent microbatches that require fragmented replay) and emit per-route. This will help triage on production. (owner: Jonah)
4) Bench persistent-kernel memory delta across all supported instance types and add an autoscaler guard that prevents persistent mode on low-memory nodes. (owner: Marina)
5) Create an A/B rollout for stream-priority bump only on dedicated pools with isolated workloads. Observe cross-tenant interference for 48h. (owner: SRE/infra)

Immediate short-term mitigation (low risk):
- Enable prewarm graphs by default for hosted API routes where mean token length variance < 20% and where we observe graph_fragment_rate > 5%. This is a conservative heuristic to reduce on-demand recapture.

Notes / rough logs: (copy-paste from capture)
- Capture 2025-12-09T16:12:22Z: NVTX stack snippet: SERVICE_ENTRY -> BATCHER_HANDOFF -> KERNEL_LAUNCH_PREP (132us) -> CUDA_GRAPH_REPLAY (1.2ms) -> POST_REPLAY_SYNC (sync call 0.45ms) -> next kernel
- SM occupancy sample: before gap 71%, during gap 9%, after kernel 69%
- Kernel launch counts: expected 1.00 per microbatch, observed 1.12 on average for this workload

Open questions / discussion points:
- Is the baseline conservative sync required for correctness, or was it added as a historical safety net? (I suspect the latter; needs code owner confirmation)
- Are there other components that do implicit synchronizations (Python GC, logging flushes) that line up with the observed gaps?
- For dedicated pools, could we reserve a small fraction of high-priority GPU capacity for copy/transfer streams to avoid cross-stream preemption?

Files attached / capturable artifacts (placed in perf bucket):
- nsight_capture_batch_2025-12-09a.qdrep (60s steady window)
- kernel_histogram_best.csv (per-microbatch kernel size histogram)
- microbench_results_2025-12-10.csv
- short screen recordings: gap_examples.mp4 (timestamps annotated)

Draft notes / ideas for engineering patch (very rough):
- Introduce GraphCache keyed by (model_id, microbatch_bucket, quant_profile). On microbatch path: if cache hit and graph_valid -> do pinned replay. If cache miss but microbatch_bucket within allowed variance -> kick async recapture in background and use fallback path for first few requests.
- Replace broad cudaStreamSynchronize with a small host-side timestamp fence: post-replay write a small 8-byte counter via cudaMemcpyAsync to host pinned memory and poll for value instead of full sync. Requires testing on all supported drivers.

Owners and next sync:
- Owners: Priya (runtime changes + sync replacement), Evan (graph cache/prewarm), Jonah (telemetry), Marina (memory/host sizing), SRE (A/B and infra).
- Next sync: 2025-12-17 internal perf meeting, bring Nsight captures and microbench results for before/after PR.

If anyone wants the raw qdrep + CSVs, ping me or check the perf bucket (linked in Confluence page). Also want code owners to review the conservative sync call path: file runtime/batcher/launch.cpp (lines ~340-380 in the captured commit).

Notes-to-self (todo list):
- Add unit test to simulate concurrent copy + launch streams and assert no extra sync needed (or that we detect regressions)
- Run persistent-kernel smoke across all CUDA versions we support (12.x, 13.x when available)
- Add guardrail in the scheduling config to disable stream-priority bump unless node is dedicated
